display: Rio de Janeiro — CCR Barcas (Guanabara Bay Ferries)

partner_context.their_ambition: CCR Barcas runs the public ferries across Guanabara Bay — the water link that spares the Rio–Niterói Bridge and the bay's chronic congestion, carrying commuters from central Rio to Niterói and the bay's islands every day. The ambition is a faster, cleaner, more reliable bay crossing as Rio decarbonises.
partner_context.where_navier_fits: Navier is the zero-emission, foiling upgrade to a network CCR Barcas already runs. The same crossings — Praça XV to Niterói, Charitas, Paquetá and Cocotá — flown clear of the water: faster bay crossings, near-silent and low-wake, with no diesel on one of Brazil's busiest public waterways.

hero.eyebrow: Authority proposal · Rio de Janeiro, Brazil · CCR Barcas
hero.title: Navier × CCR Barcas — Guanabara Bay, on foils
hero.subtitle: A zero-emission foiling layer on the bay ferries: faster crossings from central Rio to Niterói and the islands, cleaner air, and real relief from the Rio–Niterói Bridge.
hero.what_we_do_together: CCR Barcas brings the Guanabara Bay ferry network, the terminals and the public concession; Navier brings the foiling-electric fleet, captain training and certification path. Together we run the same bay the city depends on — faster, quieter and zero-emission — decarbonising Brazil's busiest public crossing.

why_now: The Praça XV–Niterói ferry is one of the highest-frequency public water crossings in Brazil, and Rio de Janeiro State targets carbon neutrality by 2050. The demand and the decarbonisation mandate exist today — a foiling-electric layer is the fast, clean next step for the bay's busiest crossings.
multimodal_fit: Navier slots into the existing CCR Barcas network — the Praça XV hub in central Rio, the Niterói terminals at Arariboia and Charitas, and the island terminals at Paquetá and Cocotá — taking the high-frequency commuter crossings while conventional ferries keep heavier runs. Commuters step from bus and metro at Praça XV straight onto a foil across the bay.

differentiation.why_navier: The platform is proven in service and purpose-built for exactly this job: 10x more efficient than a planing hull, low-wake (better for a busy, ecologically-stressed bay), near-silent, and zero-emission. It decarbonises Brazil's busiest public bay crossing while cutting journey times on the water.

objections.concern: Can a foiling ferry handle the open water of Guanabara Bay?
objections.response: Pioneer II needs only a berth pedestal at the existing terminals, flies above the bay chop for a smoother ride, and its low wake is gentler on a busy, ecologically-stressed bay.

objections.concern: Is this affordable for a public concession?
objections.response: Foiling-electric is ~10x more efficient than a diesel planing hull, so fuel — the largest operating cost — falls sharply; the same concession budget runs more frequent crossings.

objections.concern: Does this replace the ferries people rely on?
objections.response: No — it's a faster layer above them. Conventional ferries keep running underneath; the foiling fleet adds speed and zero-emission capacity on the busiest crossings.

the_ask.navier_brings: The software-defined foiling-electric fleet, captain training, and the maintenance and certification path, aligned to Brazilian maritime authority (Marinha do Brasil) requirements.
the_ask.partner_brings: The Guanabara Bay ferry route map, the terminals, and the public concession's service plan.
the_ask.next_step: Pick the first bay crossing — most likely Praça XV–Niterói or Charitas — for a foiling-electric public pilot.

close.body: CCR Barcas already carries Rio and Niterói across Guanabara Bay every day. Navier is how the bay's busiest crossings get faster and cleaner — giving every commuter a quick, quiet, zero-emission ride across the water, and decarbonising one of Brazil's busiest public waterways.
